title: Explain how you take a Java banking microservice from source code to running in production using Docker multi-stage builds, Kubernetes deployment, a CI/CD pipeline, and the Maven build lifecycle. Cover Docker, K8s, Helm, CI/CD, Maven vs Gradle, Git branching, SonarQube, and zero-downtime deployment.
shortTitle: DevOps — Docker multi-stage, K8s deployment, CI/CD pipeline, Maven lifecycle

s1_definition.profdef: Docker packages the application plus the Java runtime into an immutable image. A multi-stage build compiles the code in one stage using a full JDK, then copies only the finished JAR into a slim JRE stage so the final image stays small. Kubernetes orchestrates that image: it manages Deployments (replicas and rolling updates), Services (load balancing), ConfigMaps and Secrets (configuration), the HorizontalPodAutoscaler (automatic scaling), and health probes (liveness and readiness). A CI/CD pipeline automates the path from a Git push through build, test, static analysis with SonarQube, Docker image build and push, and finally a rolling deploy to Kubernetes. The Maven lifecycle runs the fixed phases validate, compile, test, package, verify, install, and deploy.
s1_definition.analogy: Think of the National Bank of India building a new SIP investment counter. Docker is like sealing the entire counter, the staff, and all the tools into one portable shipping container so it runs exactly the same in every branch. The multi-stage build is like assembling the counter in a big workshop with every heavy tool, then shipping only the finished, lightweight counter to the branch. Kubernetes is the branch manager who decides how many counters to open, opens a fresh one before closing an old one so customers are never turned away, and watches each counter's health. The CI/CD pipeline is the automatic quality-control line: when Rajesh the developer submits a change, it is built, tested, inspected, and rolled out to real branches without anyone manually copying files.
s1_definition.oneliner: Docker multi-stage for small images, Kubernetes for orchestration with probes and an autoscaler, and a CI/CD pipeline that automates build, test, and deploy so no human touches production by hand.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Docker packages the application plus the Java runtime into an immutable image. A multi-stage build compiles the code in one stage using a full JDK, then copies only the finished JAR into a slim JRE stage so the final image stays small. Kubernetes orchestrates that image: it manages Deployments (replicas and rolling updates), Services (load balancing), ConfigMaps and Secrets (configuration), the HorizontalPodAutoscaler (automatic scaling), and health probes (liveness and readiness). A CI/CD pipeline automates the path from a Git push through build, test, static analysis with SonarQube, Docker image build and push, and finally a rolling deploy to Kubernetes. The Maven lifecycle runs the fixed phases validate, compile, test, package, verify, install, and deploy.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Think of the National Bank of India building a new SIP investment counter. Docker is like sealing the entire counter, the staff, and all the tools into one portable shipping container so it runs exactly the same in every branch. The multi-stage build is like assembling the counter in a big workshop with every heavy tool, then shipping only the finished, lightweight counter to the branch. Kubernetes is the branch manager who decides how many counters to open, opens a fresh one before closing an old one so customers are never turned away, and watches each counter's health. The CI/CD pipeline is the automatic quality-control line: when Rajesh the developer submits a change, it is built, tested, inspected, and rolled out to real branches without anyone manually copying files.

**One line to remember:** Docker multi-stage for small images, Kubernetes for orchestration with probes and an autoscaler, and a CI/CD pipeline that automates build, test, and deploy so no human touches production by hand.

sections.s2_technical:
A Docker image is built from a `Dockerfile`, which is a recipe of layers. The most important production technique is the multi-stage build. In the first stage you use a heavy `eclipse-temurin:21-jdk-alpine` base image that contains the full compiler and Maven, and you run `mvn clean package` to produce the JAR. In the second stage you start fresh from a slim `eclipse-temurin:21-jre-alpine` image that has only the runtime, and you copy just the JAR across with `COPY --from=builder`. For example, `COPY --from=builder /build/target/sip-investment-service-1.0.0.jar app.jar` brings only the finished artifact, so the final image does not carry the compiler, Maven, or the source code. This typically cuts the image from around 600 megabytes down to under 200 megabytes, which means faster pulls and a smaller attack surface.

Kubernetes runs that image through several objects. A Deployment describes the desired state, such as `replicas: 3`, and Kubernetes keeps exactly that many Pods alive. The rolling update strategy with `maxUnavailable: 0` and `maxSurge: 1` means Kubernetes starts a new Pod and waits for it to become ready before terminating an old one, giving zero downtime. A readiness probe like `httpGet: /actuator/health/readiness` tells Kubernetes when a Pod can receive traffic, and a liveness probe like `httpGet: /actuator/health/liveness` tells it when to restart a stuck Pod. The HorizontalPodAutoscaler watches CPU and scales the Pod count, for example from three up to ten when average CPU crosses seventy percent.

Configuration is injected, never baked in. A ConfigMap holds non-secret values and a Secret holds passwords, and the container reads them through `envFrom`. In Spring Boot these arrive as environment variables that override `application.yml`, so the same image runs in dev and prod with different config.

The CI/CD pipeline ties it together. In GitHub Actions a `build-test` job runs `mvn clean verify` to compile and run unit and integration tests, then `mvn sonar:sonar` for static analysis where a quality gate can fail the build if coverage drops or critical bugs appear. A `docker-push` job builds the image tagged with the commit SHA and pushes it to a registry. A `deploy` job runs `kubectl set image` to trigger the rolling update. The commit SHA tag is important because it makes every deploy traceable to an exact commit and makes rollback a one-line change.

The Maven lifecycle is a fixed ordered sequence of phases, and running a later phase runs all earlier ones. `mvn validate` checks the project is correct, `mvn compile` compiles sources, `mvn test` runs unit tests, `mvn package` creates the JAR, `mvn verify` runs integration tests and quality checks, `mvn install` places the artifact in your local repository, and `mvn deploy` publishes it to a shared repository. A senior nuance is that `mvn clean package -DskipTests` is used inside the Docker build stage because tests already ran in the CI `verify` job, so you do not want to run them twice. Compared to Gradle, Maven uses a rigid XML lifecycle that is predictable and easy to standardize across teams, while Gradle uses a Groovy or Kotlin DSL with a build cache that is faster and more flexible but needs more discipline.

On Git branching, the trunk-based model is common in banking platform teams: short-lived feature branches like `feature/sip-returns` branch off `main`, a pull request triggers the CI checks, and after review the branch merges back and CD deploys. This keeps `main` always releasable.
sections.s3_banking:
The National Bank of India is launching a new SIP investment service where customers like Rajesh and Priya set up monthly mutual-fund investments. The development team needs this service to run reliably in production and to be deployed many times a day without customers ever seeing an outage.

Problem 1 — The service used to be deployed by copying a JAR to a server by hand, and the server had the wrong Java version, so it crashed on startup. This is exactly what Docker solves. By packaging the exact Java runtime and the JAR into one immutable image, the service runs identically on every machine, removing the "it worked on my laptop" problem.

Problem 2 — The old Docker image was almost 700 megabytes because it shipped the compiler and the full source tree, so pulling it during a deploy was slow and it had more software that attackers could exploit. This is exactly what a multi-stage build solves. We compile in a heavy JDK stage and then copy only the finished JAR into a slim JRE stage, producing a small, lean image.

Problem 3 — When the team deployed, they would stop the old version first, so for thirty seconds customers got errors. This is exactly what Kubernetes rolling updates with readiness probes solve. Kubernetes brings up a new Pod, waits until its readiness probe passes, and only then removes an old Pod, so there is always a healthy counter open.

Problem 4 — On salary day, thousands of customers set up SIPs at once and three Pods were not enough, so the service slowed to a crawl. This is exactly what the HorizontalPodAutoscaler solves. It watches CPU and automatically adds Pods up to a limit, then removes them when the rush is over.

Problem 5 — A bad change once reached production because no one ran the tests. This is exactly what a CI/CD pipeline with a SonarQube quality gate solves. Every change is automatically built, tested, and inspected before it can be deployed.

The code and configuration will include: a `Dockerfile` with two stages, a Kubernetes `deployment.yml` with rolling update and probes, an `hpa.yml` autoscaler, a GitHub Actions `ci-cd.yml` pipeline with build-test, docker-push, and deploy jobs, an `application.yml` showing injected config, and the Spring Boot source for the SIP service itself (entity, repository, service, controller) plus a Testcontainers integration test. The demo step is the full journey: Rajesh pushes code, CI builds and tests it, the image is pushed, and Kubernetes rolls it out with zero downtime.

sections.s4e_build:
```bash
# Maven lifecycle
mvn clean                  # delete target/
mvn compile                # compile sources
mvn test                   # run unit tests
mvn package                # create JAR
mvn verify                 # run integration tests
mvn install                # install to local repo
mvn clean package -DskipTests  # fast build

# Docker multi-stage build
docker build -t bank/sip-investment-service:1.0.0 .
docker run -p 8113:8113 -e DB_HOST=host.docker.internal bank/sip-investment-service:1.0.0

# K8s deploy
kubectl apply -f k8s/

# Test
curl http://localhost:8113/api/v1/sip/summary/SAV2001

# Git workflow (trunk-based)
git checkout -b feature/sip-returns
git commit -m "feat: add SIP return calculation"
git push -u origin feature/sip-returns
# → PR → CI runs (build + test + sonar) → merge → CD deploys
```
sections.s5_journey:
Input data: Rajesh the developer pushes a commit to the branch `feature/sip-returns` with commit SHA `a1b2c3d`, and the target is to get this running in the three-Pod Kubernetes deployment with zero downtime.

Step 1: The push reaches GitHub, which triggers the `ci-cd.yml` workflow. At this point the data is the source code at commit `a1b2c3d` sitting in the GitHub runner. Nothing is deployed yet.

Step 2: The `build-test` job checks out the code and runs `mvn clean verify`. The sources are compiled, unit tests and the Testcontainers integration test run against a throwaway PostgreSQL, and a JAR is produced in the runner. The source has now become a tested artifact.

Step 3: The same job runs `mvn sonar:sonar`. The code is analyzed and the quality gate checks coverage and critical bugs. If the gate fails, the pipeline stops here and nothing moves forward, so the production state stays unchanged.

Step 4: The `docker-push` job runs only on `main`. It builds the image using the multi-stage `Dockerfile`: stage one compiles with the JDK, stage two copies only the JAR into the slim JRE image. The artifact has now become an immutable image tagged `bank/sip-investment-service:a1b2c3d`, which is pushed to the registry.

Step 5: The `deploy` job runs `kubectl set image` with the SHA tag. Kubernetes sees the Deployment's desired image changed and begins a rolling update.

Step 6: Kubernetes starts a fourth Pod (`maxSurge: 1`) with the new image. It waits for that Pod's readiness probe at `/actuator/health/readiness` to pass. Only when the new Pod reports ready does Kubernetes terminate one old Pod, honoring `maxUnavailable: 0`. It repeats until all three Pods run the new image. Throughout, at least three healthy Pods serve traffic, so Rajesh's and Priya's requests never fail.

Step 7: On salary day, CPU across the Pods climbs above seventy percent. The HorizontalPodAutoscaler adds Pods up to ten. When the rush ends and CPU falls, it scales back down to three.

sections.s6_takeaway:
In my banking project I package every microservice as a Docker image using a multi-stage build. The first stage uses a full Java Development Kit with Maven to compile and produce the JAR, and the second stage starts from a slim Java Runtime Environment image and copies only the finished JAR across. This keeps the production image small and lean because it does not carry the compiler or the source code, which means faster pulls and a smaller attack surface.

I run these images on Kubernetes. A Deployment keeps a fixed number of replicas alive, and I configure a rolling update with maximum unavailable set to zero so Kubernetes always starts a new Pod and waits for its readiness probe to pass before it terminates an old Pod. That gives genuine zero-downtime deploys. A liveness probe lets Kubernetes restart a stuck Pod, and a HorizontalPodAutoscaler watches CPU and automatically adds Pods during peak load, such as salary day when thousands of customers set up investments at once, then scales back down afterward.

Everything is automated through a continuous integration and delivery pipeline. When a developer pushes a change, the pipeline compiles the code, runs the unit and integration tests, and runs a SonarQube static analysis with a quality gate that blocks the deploy if coverage drops or critical bugs appear. Only then does it build the image, tag it with the exact commit identifier, push it to the registry, and trigger the Kubernetes rolling update. Tagging by commit makes every deploy traceable and makes rollback a single line.

Underneath all of this is the Maven lifecycle, which runs the fixed phases of validate, compile, test, package, verify, install, and deploy, where each phase runs every earlier one. I keep secrets like the database password in a Kubernetes Secret rather than baking them into the image, and I inject configuration through environment variables so the same image runs unchanged across every environment. This whole setup is what lets the bank deploy many times a day with confidence and without any customer ever seeing an outage.

---

keyPoints: Maven: convention over configuration, lifecycle phases
Gradle: flexible, Groovy/Kotlin DSL, faster incremental builds
mvn install: compile+test+package+install to local repo
Dependency management: BOM for consistent versions
